title: The Oncological Impact of Low Vascular Tie After Surgery for Upper and Middle Rectal Cancer: Is a Low Vascular Tie Enough? Seven-Year Follow-Up in a Single Centre Slovakian Cohort
content:
Objective:
The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of low vascular ligation on oncological outcomes in upper and middle rectal cancer surgery.
Despite significant progress in colorectal surgery, many questions remain unanswered, and there is ongoing debate about optimal management. One of the key issues is the height of vascular ligation of arteria mesenterica inferior (IMA) during rectal resection. Many believe that high vascular ligation is beneficial from an oncological point of view in terms of survival. However, the available data indicate that the height of ligation is not decisive in terms of its oncological impact, as the number of lymph nodes harvested (minimum are 12 lymph nodes) with high vascular ligation is not significantly greater than the number harvested with low vascular ligation.
Methods:
This study identified and followed all stage I–III/b rectal cancer patients with a tumor in the upper or middle rectum who underwent abdominal surgery with curative intent between 2013 and 2017 at the 3rd Surgical Clinic of Comenius University in Bratislava. In this study we included 96 patient, consisting of 44 females and 52 males and they were subdivided into two groups based on the tumor's distance from the anus: the first group included upper rectal tumors (12-16 cm from the anus), and the second group included middle rectal tumors (6-12 cm from the anus). Preoperative tumor evaluation included a physical examination with a digital rectal exam and anoscopy, serum CEA and CA19-9, total colonoscopy with biopsy, pelvic MRI, and CT. The primary outcome was cancer-specific survival, while the secondary outcomes included overall and relative survival, locoregional and distant recurrence, and lymph node harvest.
Results:
The study evaluated 96 patients with rectal tumors located in the upper and middle parts of the rectum who underwent MRI examination followed by surgical resection. In all the patients, due to anatomical conditions, a low vascular ligation was performed with subsequent anastomosis.
Conclusion:
In this study, low ligation did not influence any patient-oriented oncological outcomes in comparison with the literature. The literature suggests that high vascular ligation can harvest more lymph nodes (1-2), but it does not affect survival. Therefore, the height of the ligation should be determined during surgery.
